utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. According to the clock in this courtroom, we start with 20 minutes to 9.00. I would appreciate if it could be adjusted soon. The Chamber is privy of a conversation between the parties who would continue or start cross-examination today. From what we've seen it seems that the party -- that the Stanisic Defence does not oppose a suggestion made by the Prosecution to continue -- or to start its cross-examination now. There was something about the number of documents. Has that been resolved?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, that hasn't. We didn't oppose in principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But we wanted a clear indication from the Prosecution concerning the amount of new documents they wished to use because that, in our submission, impacts upon whether the Defence beginning at this stage would in fact save the time that the Prosecution claim it would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The usual order of cross-examination was varied for a specific reason and that was because the Stanisic Defence was unable to communicate with Mr. Stanisic. Now, they asserted they needed a week's time and they've now had that time, so the reason for changing the order no longer exists, so in our submission we should revert to the usual order. Now the Defence raise a new and separate issue; that is, the Prosecution's use of documents not yet in evidence during cross-examination. They're attempting now to argue that as a basis for continuing with the inverted order of cross-examination. So in our submission as this issue would not have been a sufficient reason to reverse the order in the first place, it should not be considered to be a reason to maintain the reversed order now, and I do believe that it will save time -- additional time in cross-examination for them to proceed first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. They do not only attempt to argue but even argue. That's ... Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm not sure what to say. The Prosecution are clearly unwilling to indicate how many new exhibits they intend to use. And if they use 48 new documents, that will give rise to a multitude of new issues which will then have to be dealt with afterwards. I mean, if -- I don't want to make a big fuss of this, and if -- if -- I'm ready to proceed if that's what Your Honours want, but it would have been useful to have an indication from the Prosecution. But I'm happy to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, could you give us any indication .

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. It's exactly as I communicated to the Defence by e-mail. I itemised the individual documents that I planned to call up individually, and I explained that with respect to the documents underlying the charts, the three charts, I intend to deal with those as a whole. That was -- that's -- as clear an indication as I can give in advance as possible. That is precisely, at the moment, what I -- what I plan to do. And the decision of -- use and tendering, in my view, is two different issues. The use -- we have a perfect right to use whatever we -- we seek to use. The tendering we will decide at the tail-end of the -- of the witness's testimony, what we seek to tender, based on his responses to the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, the Chamber is not blind for the problems you may face, but the basic issue that the usual order is Defence first and then Prosecution, that is what makes us conclude that you're the one now to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we start, I would like to remind you, Mr. Milosevic, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given at the beginning of your testimony. But that would have been clear to you anyhow. Mr. Jordash [sic], you have followed the discussion, whether Ms. Marcus would continue and then conclude her cross-examination or whether, which is the usual order, Mr. Jordash would now start his cross-examination. You have heard the decision. So it will first be Mr. Jordash, then the conclusion of Ms. Marcus, her cross-examination, and then possibly re-examination. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: First of all, Professor, I'd like to deal with the issue concerning the Supreme Court of Serbia's participation in the interception of telephones and such. You indicated that - am I correct? - that the rules indicated that that should take place, that the Supreme Court should be approached to give approval before intrusive surveillance of certain kinds took place; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're absolutely right. The president of the Supreme Court or a judge that he designates takes a decision. That's the procedure. The decision concerns the Ministry of Interior. Or, rather, he is the only one who can suggest that such a decision can be taken, and then the court has the power to take such a decision. I think that's what it says in the text. The service can provide these suggestions that SDB most frequently, but only the minister can officially submit such a suggestion to the court. So the court has absolute control over the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now you fairly said that you were talking about the rules and not necessarily the practice and that you were not aware of whether this, during the relevant period, had been followed to the letter or not. But what you did discuss --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- at, Your Honours, page 18295 --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- was what I interpreted as a culture within the state security. And, in particular, a culture arising from the misbehaviour of a chief of police who was accused of intercepting the period of time the republic, Tito, and the president of the party. Sorry, the president of the republic and the president of the party, which was Tito. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I do. The Brioni Plenum is what is concerned. That is the name that is usually given to that event. I'm very familiar with all the details concerning that affair.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Am I correct, before we go into the details, that what you were attempting to say was that it was well-known and a part of the culture within the DB, by the time we get to 1991, that there was real potential for the misuse of intrusive surveillance arising from this particular affair, which we'll go into in a moment?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was such a culture, as you say. Everyone was cautious. They were well aware of the fact that anything that deviated from the rules and regulations could be a big problem for those who were involved. Everyone was, as a result, very cautious. I stated here that there were no affairs at the time. There was one later in the year 2000 and it doesn't concern anyone here. It concerns different people. I can give you the details if you like. But at any time there weren't any affairs in public view, and there were no doubts that anyone had about such affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I limit the culture too much because the culture, in fact, was a culture which infected everyone who might be the subject of surveillance if Tito, the logic went, could be intrusively bugged then so could Milosevic, so could any of the leadership, and it was that awareness which was -- defined the culture within the DB and outside of the DB. Am I summarising things correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, the basis for all this is -- I mean, in view of the expertise of the witness, I really have -- the culture, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I'm referring to what the witness earlier said about at, Your Honours, page 18926, where he talks about the Brioni Plenum case where he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. But then to create the culture was major, mainly defined by the -- that requires a thorough in-depth study of all that, instead of a kind of subjective feeling of what the culture is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, you'll understand that it's -- it's all of such an abstract and vague nature that one wonders what it is exactly based on more than subjective feelings. And, of course, one or two incidents which may have taken place. I mean, in order to find out what the feeling is within an organisation, you would have to interview persons on that. If you want to really establish something in a -- in an accepted psychological or sociological methodology, but it seems that that is not the basis of the answers of the witness in his report in this respect on the matter you just touched upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I will try and have the witness explain why he concluded that there was this caution, at least, that was exercised in these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whether it's mainly on the basis of subjective feelings and speaking now and then, not in a systematic way, with a few persons or whether it was based on more.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You followed the discussion, Professor?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's try to understand this as briefly as we can. You said at page 18926 last week: "... but in Serbia much caution was exercised in the matter, and people are very wary of violating the rules on interception." What's your source of information? Why did you testify that way?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's quite simply the case. If you like, there is a certain culture as you say, that existed in the service, in the department and outside. The service wasn't involved with politics and politicians. They didn't want to mix the department and politics. Those are two different things. That was the first matter. And then, secondly, secret resources used by the SDB shouldn't be used without good grounds. They should be used in a restrictive manner. One learned from the past, because there was an accusation that Muslims used -- well, I don't know to need go into further details, do I then?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, but I'm trying to understand how you came to the conclusion that there was a culture within the service at around the time of these events, in the -- in the early 1990s. Where do you -- why do you make that -- why did you arrive at that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to determine such facts, psychological facts, but you determine them on the basis of external indicators. As you know, the fact that there was no affair that broke out in public view speaks for itself. Later such things occurred but not between the period 1991 to 1995. Naturally, the presidents and the prime minister of the SRJ -- SRY were intercepted, their conversations were intercepted at Karadjordjevo, but this has nothing to do with this story. But in Serbia itself there were no problems in public view. At least I wasn't aware of any such problems, and it's on that basis that I have drawn this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So it's simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, if you would not mind. I would like to analyse your answer. You say the -- you know the fact there was no affair that broke out in public view speaks for itself. Now, that's totally unclear to me, especially if I listen to that together with your last sentence: "But in Serbia itself, there were no problems in public view. At least I wasn't aware of any such problems, and it's on that basis that I've drawn my conclusions." So whether something did not happen or whether you were not aware it to happen is unclear in your answer. You were not aware, which can mean two things: That it didn't happen; or that it happened, but that you were not aware. That's exactly also the problem with your answer, that the fact that there was no affair speaks for itself. It doesn't speak for itself at all, I would say, because if an affair does not break out in public, it can mean that there is nothing to break out in public or that there were other factors, which, although there was an affair, it did not break out in public. So, therefore, from an expert point of view, your answer, both in the beginning and at the end, clearly demonstrate what the problem is; that is, that without thorough investigation of certain matters, that you wouldn't know. You may have an impression. You may be aware of certain facts, you may not be aware of other facts. That's exactly my intellectual problem with this specific answer and that it was -- it was that point, Mr. Jordash, that I addressed in my previous observation. If you would like to further clarify your answer, fine. But I think it would be good for everyone to know that your answer exactly demonstrates what I earlier expressed as being my problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may -- although we are not in a debate, I give you a fair opportunity to -- to bring to our attention whatever you think relevant in relation to the general observation I made earlier and in relation to the answer I just tried to analyse.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is my subjective impression. I didn't carry out an investigation. I didn't carry out a poll. But as a citizen who lived there at the time, I can't remember any affairs. Someone would have had to bring such cases to court or would have had to appear in the press. I can't remember any such cases. But what I have been speaking about is the impression I gained at the time, and that is what I have conveyed to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's just continue this subject but moving it along, hopefully. Paragraph 161 of your report. Let's have a look at that time. I want to examine just briefly what controls existed in relation to the work of the state security at the relevant time. 161 deals with the Council for the Protection of the Constitutional Order being a working body of the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Serbia. And paragraph 163 concerns the Law on Control of the State Security Service. Did either of these entities or the council or the law have a supervisory role over such things as intrusive surveillance?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now the Council for the Protection of the Constitutional Order, did that exist in 1991 through to -- let's just limit ourselves to the indictment period, but 1995/1996?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question concerns the Council for the protection or the comission for control. Could you please repeat your question, because I'm not sure what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Paragraph 161 deals with the Council for the Protection of the Constitutional Order. Let me try to break this down. Did that council have a role to play in supervising the legality of intrusive surveillance conducted by the State Security Service in 1991 through to 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And who was on that council?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The members were prominent politicians at the time. Civil servants.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Presumably, then, in 1991 onwards, as the breakdown occurred, these were prominent politicians close to Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the parliament there are various politicians. Milosevic didn't appoint members of the parliament. This was something that was decided at freely held elections. The majority appoints a government. I don't really understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think I've taken that as far as I want to. But the law -- did the council have a role in ensuring that the Law on the Control of the State Security Service was complied with?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was its purpose, amongst other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So do we take your answer that you gave a few moments ago when the learned Judge was querying your answer, do we take your answer to be that you would have expected this council to have closely supervised whether the state security was conducting intrusive surveillance within the law, and you would have expected that, if they hadn't been, this council would have seen that and been concerned about that, given that they, themselves, might be targets?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, if you wouldn't mind, a few matters you touched upon. The first was the role in the intrusive surveillance. What the role was has not been further elaborated so we do not know. Then, second, who were members of the council. They apparently were politicians. Then you took it to whether they were close to President Milosevic. We have no answer to that. Neither do we know how they were exactly appointed because that's not described, I think, in 161 and 162. So we now know that members of parliament were elected. That doesn't come as a shocking, new, information. But all the other issues was touched upon. Apparently you have some concerns about it or at least you would like to know more about it, but whenever the question about the role, about how were people of the council appointed, was there any selective methods that those close to the political position of President Milosevic would be the ones on -- on the council, we still do not know. So everything --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise. I think I'm just trying to go too quickly today, and I think you're absolutely right. I'm missing bringing some clarification to these issues, and I'll certainly do my best --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you want us to consider it, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- please give us the information through the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's try to -- if I can try to be more direct and you can try to be more direct in your answer, and we can try to assist the Chamber in understanding these issues. Did the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia appoint the members of the council?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assembly appointed the members of the commission. For overseeing the State Security Service, that is. And that is what I meant. That's the one that dealt with direct control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I thought we were dealing with the council; that is, 161 and 162 in the report. It now appears that apparently the witness is talking about the commission, which is described in 163 and following, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what he -- you asked about members of the council. I took it that your question was about the council described in 161. And then the witness said the assembly appointed the member of the commission for overseeing State Security Service. That is a commission which I find in 163.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, I think we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there seems to be a -- question and the answer have not got much to do with each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's focus -- let's try to do this systematically, Mr. Milosevic. Paragraph 161 is talking about the council. What do you know about how the council was elected in 1991 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know that. I did not really deal with the council except I mentioned it here. As a matter of fact, I don't even know -- well, I can talk about the commission that dealt with this directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. So your previous answers concerning the control of the State Security Service were intended to apply --

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- you were talking about the commission and not the council.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. So let's go to paragraph 164 of your report. "The assembly of the Republic of Serbia set up the commission for the Control of the State Security Service." What do you know about the way in which the president and six members were elected by the assembly? Do you know anything about how that election took place?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we get the years that we're talking about for this commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think in earlier questions Mr. Jordash always talked about 1991 to 1995/1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. And that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is the time-frame in which I understood all these questions to be put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Professor, what do you know about the election of the president and the six members by the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were elected from the ranks of the assembly delegates. I mentioned these 185 in a footnote. And I even said which house of parliament they belonged to. So they were appointed by the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And do you --

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is from 1986 until 1990. And that was further elaborated by the rules of procedure, as is written here, of the Republic of Serbia. So every year in the rules of procedure, it was clearly stated how this would be done. The rules of procedure are the valid document on the basis of which all of this is done. And, actually, that is all written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What about 1990 to 1995? What was the situation there with the commission? You haven't spoken about that in your report. Do you know anything of it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the Law on Interior, from 1989 the Assembly of Serbia was supposed to supervise the work of, et cetera, et cetera. And a commission was to be established. I assume that it was done in the same way. However, in the rules of procedure, I did not find a specific elaboration of that. It would only be logical for it to be completely identical, but I truly haven't found anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But why do you limit it, then, to 1990? Are you saying that the law came to an end in 1990 or the last law that -- or the last regulations you found in place were those that were promulgated in 1990? I don't understand why you haven't considered this post-1990.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I found rules of procedure of the assembly only up to 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So it's not that you found a set of rules saying it all no longer applies post-1990. It's just the latest rules you found related to 1990.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the way the commission operated post-1990?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it operated the same way it did until then. That is to say that they had the right to ask for any file, to look at any file. They could check things any way they wanted to. The service had to comply, of course. There couldn't have been any difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, Professor, you say there couldn't have been any difference, but I want to make sure we're dealing in facts. Do you, in fact, know anything about the work of the commission from your own personal observation, from speaking to others? If you don't, you don't. That's fine. But I want to make sure we're dealing in facts.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the commission could operate only in that way. I don't see how else it could operate. How else it could have insight without having access to files, documents, et cetera. But, indeed, I did not take part in the work of the conference. I am not a fact witness. I was not in attendance when the commission met.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, could I ask -- Do you know how the commission was composed, on from 1990? Who were the members? I mean, for the first -- for the first, you said you said that in the footnote. But for the others, you didn't know who the members were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you know whether they met, or whether they frequently met, or whether they actually did send reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I just take instructions, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know anything about at this -- and, again, we're talking about 1991 to 1995, do you know anything about a board of security within the assembly, where the -- which the minister of the interior had to report to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. That was the parliamentary committee that was in charge of overseeing all the security services and the entire field of internal affairs in Serbia. So this was the parliamentary committee that received reports from the minister of the interior, and the minister submitted these reports on the basis of the reports that he received from the RDB and the SDB. I assume that your question pertains only to the SDB part. So that is what was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, you asked something. Where do we find this parliamentary committee or board of security, as Mr. Jordash mentioned? Where do we find it in your report, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is mentioned in several places, Your Honour, and I'll try to find them now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you remember the official name, then we could easily do a search through your report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Committee for Security and Defence. Or the Parliamentary Committee for Security and Defence. And I think it's mentioned in several places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I search for "parliamentary" I have difficulties in -- but I may have misspelled, as a matter of fact, in my search.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Committee for security," "security committee." Those are the key words. So perhaps it could be found on the basis of those key words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps I may be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 166 of the report, footnote 179.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, 166, we dealt with that, because that was the subject where we had to establish that the witness did not know about the functioning of the commission. But if that's the same commission, then I'm a bit surprised by the question, after Mr. Jordash had taken instructions. Because 166 we dealt with in quite some detail. The missing further rules of procedure on from 1990. So, therefore, if that's the same, then I'm really surprised by the formulation of the question. Because it apparently was seeking something different from what we had discussed and where the witness had no knowledge about the functioning of that commission. Mr. Jordash, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. I hadn't presumed that 166 was what we were talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Confusion seems to be almost complete by now. Let's -- no, no, I'm not blaming you Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I contributed to the confusion. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But let's try to reduce it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Perhaps, Professor, you could look for that during a break to save you the panic at the moment. What I could ask you about, though, and we could return to this subject, is paragraph 167 where you detail a law -- the Law on the Internal Affairs, 1989, which appears to detail or mandate the assembly to set up a commission for the political control of the legality of the work of the State Security Services. Are we talking about a continuation of the commission that we were talking about in paragraph 164, or are you talking about something else here?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the wording from the law itself. De facto, that is a continuation of that control because the assembly, the highest organ of government, primarily exercises political control.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. So that's the same commission as the Commission for the Control of the State Security Service. And the 1989 law envisaged that the assembly would keep setting up that commission going forwards?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what the law says.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Let's return to this subject once you've had a chance to look through the report to identify the security commission you've referred to a moment ago. Let's go to paragraph 45 of your report. I want to understand a little more about the process by which the Kosovo province and the Vojvodina province, DBs -- or provincial DBs became part of the Serbian DB. Prior to the merging of the three DBs, did the rules envisage that they would act and conduct their work autonomously with some co-ordination through the federal DB?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The law explicitly said that the republican secretary, that is to say the minister, and the provincial secretaries, that is to say the ministers of the interior, will co-ordinate the work of the security service that is in a way that would be of interest to the entire republic protecting the constitutional order and so on and so forth. So they were supposed to act independently - but how do I put this? - in a synchronised manner. Of course, only with regard to those matters that are of interest to the entire republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So looking at paragraph 52 of your report, you speak of the change in the law adopted on the 17th of July 1991 where the three organisations would, by law, be merged, and then the second half of the paragraph states: "However, in conformity with the provisions of Article 70 of the said law, the provincial SUP, and thereby also the SDB of the Autonomous Province of Vojvodina, continued to discharge the duties entrusted them in this field pending -- pending the adoption of appropriate sub-laws on the organisation of work and staffing specifications. In this way, the State Security Service of the SUP Vojvodina continued to discharge duties entrusted it up until January 1992." Could you clarify this a little. Do you know, first of all, when these appropriate sub-laws were eventually promulgated and operative? Was that in January 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in January. Those were the regulations on the organisation and work that we discussed several times. I think that we practically lost two days analysing only those regulations. That was from 1992. So the answer to your question is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So the Vojvodina SUP remained autonomous effectively until January 1992. Maintained its own hierarchy and maintained its own annual work-plans and so on, at least on paper. That's what I'm talking about: On paper.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. They continued carrying out all their functions as they had been doing up until then. So this is the period from July 1991 until January 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now -- sorry, go on.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this has to do with all of it. Say, the secondary school for internal affairs and the post-secondary school. They all continued operating until further notice, if you will. So my response to your question is: That it was from July 1991 until January 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And let's be clear because your answer is a bit ambiguous. Are you suggesting the rules and the laws and the regulations effectively remained the same within the Vojvodina SUP; or are you suggesting the rules and the laws and the regulations, plus practice, stayed the same? Are you talking about practice here or limiting your answer to the rules and regulations?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously laws and regulations were in force. I believe that practice was in force, if you well. It wasn't possible to change it over such a short span of time. So that's the way things went on until January 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say, "It wasn't possible to change it over a short span of time. I believe that practice was in force..." Do you know it? I mean, I do understand that if the sub-laws have not been adopted that school system, for example, education, that that remained the same. But do you know whether, on the operational level, on the ground, whether they were, up till January, that they were still operating independently? Do you know anything about it? Or that it merged already. Or that -- what can you tell us about the operations on the ground during this period where the system had been changed but not all the sub-laws had been adopted? If you know. If you don't know, then tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The State Security Service can only operate on the basis of regulations on their work organisation, et cetera. Since these regulations had not been adopted yet, then the practice that existed until then was continued until the new regulations were adopted. That's what I know, as I've said several times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your answer is ambiguous again. You say the State Security Service can only operate. The question is whether they could only operate but whether you have any factual knowledge about how they did operate. Because to say that if the regulations have not been adapted, the practice was continued, that -- that requires factual knowledge of the operations themselves. Not what they should be, but how these operations took place. Do you -- could you give us examples of that? To say, Okay, look at that. Those and those operations of Vojvodina went on independently from any inference, from the branch with which it was merged once these bylaws had been adopted. Could you give us examples? Do you know anything about facts in this respect? There's no problem if you do not, but we'd just like to know whether it's your conclusion that it should have been, as you describe it here, or whether it was, as you describe it here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My conclusions are always based on the interpretation of regulations. That is to say, I have no personal knowledge of whether some operation evolved this way or some other way. I'm just saying that that is what it was like on the basis of regulations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know why there was a delay in these -- in the promulgation of sub-laws in regards to Vojvodina compared to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Kosovo SDB in a certain sense had already merged, had a different status in relation to certain events and constitutional changes that had previously taken place. This is explained in detail in my report. The service in Kosovo for well-known events, for well-known reasons, had already merged.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now the -- at the time that the Vojvodina SUP was a separate organisational unit, it had its own head of state security, according to the rules; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And its own minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And had -- the Vojvodina SUP had no obligation, according to the rules, to report to the Serbian SUP.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's interesting that in the Law on Internal Affairs the Vojvodina SUP didn't have any obligations with respect to the RSUP of Serbia. This wasn't logical, given that this was an autonomous region within a state, but it's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the Vojvodina SUP hierarchy had no obligation to -- according to the rules, to accept instructional orders from the Serbian SUP hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, no. They didn't have any such obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you able to confirm that the - and I'm sorry if I've missed this in your report - are you able to confirm -- actually, I don't need to deal with that. I was going ask you about the constitutional amendments which were necessary to allow this merger to take place, but I think that's dealt with in paragraph 50 of your report. Let's go to paragraph 22 -- 240, please, of your report. I want to deal with processing, evaluation, and analysis of operative intelligence data and reports. I want to try to understand what the rules concerning reporting envisaged in relation to the transmission of information up from the ground towards the -- and to the chief of the DB. The reports which are -- and I'm trying to paraphrase so as not to repeat, so forgive me if my language is a bit loose. But the reports which -- or the documentation produced at the ground level by operatives are, and I summarise, the primary documents?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is your question what was done with such reports?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about definitions at the moment. Documentation produced by operatives on behalf of centres, for example, documents which emerge from gathering intelligence or counter-intelligence on the ground are the primary documents within the rules of the DB; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. The general term for such information was raw information. This information hadn't been processed or verified, and it was necessary to process such information. First, to categorise the information on the basis of certain fields. It would then have to be verified, supplemented. More details would have to be added. It would have to be analysed. So in the grammatical sense of the term, one could say that this information was raw information.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And as it passed up the system -- and we'll talk about how it passed up the system towards the chief and then eventually to the political sphere, the material became less raw and more refined in terms of policy. Does that make any sense to you whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in political terms. It wasn't processed in terms of policies. I don't know where you got that idea from. Material, any kind, would arrive in the service from various sources. This was voluminous material and a selection had to be made, first of all, because some facts were incorrect, misinformation would sometimes be planted, and so on and so forth. Perhaps the sources were well intentioned but they didn't notice these deficiencies. So all these things had to be verified. However, the material was categorised on the base of their importance, not on the basis of political criteria of any kind. Politics has nothing to do with this. And it was very important to verify the facts and determine whether they were relevant with regard to posing a threat to the country. They would then be relayed to high-level organs in the service itself. The entire process was called internal intelligence [as interpreted]. Anything that was sent outside the service was called external. So some documents went up to the level of chiefs of units. Other documents were sent up to the level of the chief of the service. And only extremely important information would be sent outside the service, if the information contained warnings of some kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave. Page 26, line 13, it says "internal intelligence." I think the witness said something else, and perhaps it's not appropriate, but I would like to ask the witness to slow down because it really is difficult for the interpreters to keep up with the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I'll repeat everything that I said. I forgot that I had to speak more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me try to assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I have it on a different line. I have it on line 18: "The entire process was called internal...," and what did you then say, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's the way in which information circulated within the service. So this was internal. It didn't go outside the service. The information went from the source, so to speak, to the leadership. To the management level. But all this was done within the service. Naturally, raw source information isn't sent to higher levels. Only processed information is sent to higher levels. I think that I have stated that quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What word - and I'm not seeking for an explanation -- when you said anything and -- the entire process was called internal, and did you then use a word which may have been misunderstood or misrecorded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Information. It's a matter of providing information internally and externally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please stop. No, no. You've answered. I was only seeking the word that you used, which is "information" rather than requesting "intelligence." Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's -- I -- let's -- what -- what do you define as raw material? I know it's difficult, but try to make it concrete so that we, lay people, understand what raw material is or was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is information that the service would receive directly from a source, from a collaborator, from a citizen, from some other service, perhaps. So any initial information received. Any information that demonstrated that there might be some events of a certain kind is raw information. This information can be processed at several levels. It doesn't always have to be processed at the lowest level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I think the witness clearly explained the raw information is what comes in, which then has to be verified, has to be categorised, has to be -- et cetera, in order to -- he used that word not only today but earlier as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No. And I -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's perfectly clear and we can move on. Unless there is any specific matter in this, if I could call it this -- this verification and polishing exercise of the materials to end up at higher levels, whether that's -- any specific points needs further attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I would like to have the -- put to the witness certain descriptions of information and have him confirm or otherwise whether that would be raw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stanisic is asking for a break, but I'm in Your Honours' hands as whether I ask the next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's - not on the clock, but on my computer - is 40 minutes past 10.00, so this would be an appropriate time. And since you started a series of examples, I take it, it might be a good moment as well. We will resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to put on the record that through VWS Mr. Milosevic has delivered a list of sources, and I think he has added three appointment decisions, although in the original language attached to it. I take it that the parties have received copies of that material and that the originals are in your hands, Mr. Petrovic, at this moment, so that you can consider what to do with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. I'll agree on how we should proceed with the matter with my learned friends during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Jordash, if you are ready to proceed, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Raw material collected by operatives on the ground would include such things as reports about illegal weapons being held by a particular individual or group; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: About, for example, crimes being committed, such as murder or sexual violence on individuals, and in locations within Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And also in locations such as the SBWS and the RSK and Bosnia during the war. Would that be, in your view, raw material?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So if an extremist group in the SBWS captured and detained 12 civilians and killed them, that would be raw material which would be presumed not to go up the system to the chief of the service. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the time that the information was received, if it was received, because I'm not familiar with the circumstances, but, at the time, it would be necessary to verify that information and then to send it up the chain. The information wasn't immediately provided to the chief of the service. It had to be verified. One person couldn't do this. If you're asking me about this in general terms, well, yes, that's interesting information, but it wouldn't immediately be sent up to the chief of the service. It would first be necessary to verify and analyse the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, this is the way the rules envisaged it would happen. Stop me if I go in the --

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- wrong direction. The operative on the ground would record such information, whether through interview or personal observation or however way that information was placed into the operative report, and the operative would then give that to his superior in the centre; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The centre would then analyse that information, verify it perhaps, or seek further information, and then the head of the centre would decide whether to send that information to the relevant head of the administration dealing with that line of work?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the head of the centre would make that decision on the basis of whether the head of the centre considered that to be sufficiently important to send to the next stage of the relevant administration?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the criterion: The importance of the information. And whether it was timely, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And am I correct that importance was at the heart of whether the information continued to travel upwards towards the chief?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And importance was viewed within the lens of whether that information would, or could, impact upon the security of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Which means, of course - is this right? - that even if the information recorded the most horrific of crimes, if it didn't impact in the view of the operative or the view of the head of the centre on the security of Serbia, it would not be deemed as important, or it would be deemed as less important?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It'd depend on the circumstances of the case. But if it was important for the protection of the constitutional order and the security of Serbia, then the information in question was important. That would be the criterion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now the head of the centre who decided a particular piece of information was important would send that information to both the administration dealing with that line of work but also the 5th Administration, which was the analytical administration; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was compulsory. Everything was sent to the 5th Department. Documents were made in four copies and one was sent to them, that was compulsory and that is what the report says specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And if the head of the administration, the relevant line of work administration considered that information required to be verified or supplemented, the head of the administration would send the request back to the centre; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes. Of course, things are checked on the ground, where the information comes from. Or perhaps in some other area, if it comes from another area, but it's always checked on the ground. How shall I put this? Not in the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If the head of the administration concluded that the information was sufficiently important and sufficiently verified, the head of the administration would then send it -- there would be a presumption that the head of administration would send it to one of the chief's assistants; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the head of the administration of a particular line of work would send it to the relevant assistant. So the counter-intelligence administration would send it to the assistant of the chief, who was designated to deal with counter-intelligence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And then, at that point, the assistant of the chief would make a further analysis as to whether he felt that it was important enough to go to the next stage, which would be the deputy of the chief; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And, finally, the deputy would make that same decision and decide whether the document was -- or the information was important enough to go to the chief.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And would you have expected in that line of reporting for the information to have changed from raw material to more general - how can I put it? - general descriptions of security threats to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you meant. I didn't understand the question. Could you please be so kind as to clarify?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly. The raw material, as it works up the system - and we'll come to the 5th Administration shortly, but I want to deal with this line. The raw material, as it heads up in the system, would tend to be verified and supplemented and -- verified and supplemented according to the criteria of what this means in terms of a security threat to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So it would lose its -- perhaps it would lose some of the raw data but gain from the expert analysis of the more senior members of the service, in terms of defining how this might impact on the constitutional order.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only analysts. Also, there are some senior personnel involved. They were the ones who made these assessments. That's the criterion. The importance of the information or the data. And that is why it went through all of these instances, if you will, these filters.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. And, for example, one of the things that the process would do would be to remove all mention of the associates and sources which were not for transmission up the service, and certainly not for transmission out of the service; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would kindly ask the interpreter to repeat this once again or could you repeat your question because I don't understand what you're asking. I do apologise to the Honourable Court. However, I believe that this requires a specific answer and I'm not sure I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so. Mr. Jordash, let's try to get matters clear. I tried to understand your questions and your line of questioning. Is it that you are putting it to the witness that once this raw material was processed, was refined, was et cetera, that the factual information would more or less disappear and that the -- that the abstract description of what was at stake in terms of risks for the -- security risks, that that would remain?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm reluctant to ask -- or answer while the witness is here, because I would like to answer, obviously, but I don't want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- prejudice the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because if that would be the case, I'm not insisting on an answer, why not bluntly put that to the witness and say this and this and this?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I thought I had been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- relatively blunt. I was trying not to -- I won't be able to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could do it on the basis of an example. If you start with the murder of a group of people, terrorist acts, the question is whether that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me -- I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- information remains if it is processed, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If that's the case, then we perhaps could ask whether in the final report assessing risks for the constitutional order or security whatever, but it would still mention what it all started with. That apparently is some -- I think that's at least the impression I gained that it was a matter which you would like to be clear. I leave it at this moment in your hands, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if it's not sufficiently clarified, then of course we have an opportunity to put questions ourselves as well at later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you follow that discussion, Professor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I would prefer if, you know, put focussed questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's take an example. Perhaps we can deal with one aspect quite simply. If there was a primary document which recorded a crime which indicated, for example, that there was going to be a rebellion in Sandzak, one would expect that to go straight to the chief because it's -- or certainly to the hierarchy of the service because it's important for the security of Serbia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, in a situation where, for example, specific incidents or specific crimes are mentioned in operatives' reports and they are put together and analysed together as they go up the system, and by the time they arrive at the assistant to the chief, it's quite clear that an over -- the overall picture suggests that there's a security threat to Serbia, even if a single report or a few of the reports wouldn't in and of themselves have led to that conclusion. How much of that raw data would you expect to be presented to the upper echelons of the service and to the chief in that circumstance, where the analysis has revealed, over all, a security threat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is a story rather than a question, Mr. -- What Mr. Jordash would like to know is that if it all starts with this specific incident, the crime which was reported and which may hint at a -- a possible rebellion, so a crime committed but indicative for rebellion, would then in the -- if this would be processed further up, would only the risk of rebellion remain or would still the crime which triggered thinking about rebellion would also still be part of the report if that raw information was processed and polished and ended up at the level Mr. Jordash described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it would contain that event. Because that would indicate the possibility of a rebellion. So it would contain that. Perhaps an additional remark would be made, if necessary. So if the information is not of interest, it will not go up to higher levels, but if it is interest, as this one -- of interest, as this one is, then it would certainly go further up and contain that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And to be quite clear, if it goes up to the higher levels, both the incident triggering fear for a rebellion would still be part of the report and it would not just talk about, We fear that there may be a rebellion in the near future on the basis of information be received without even describing the incident.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the way it is, in principle. But it is possible for analytical material to be collected in several ways. However, the answer to your question is basically yes, because there has to be a factual basis for inferring something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if you say the answer is yes, you mean that still the incident would be mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you have any personal knowledge about to what extent facts which were indicative for a broader security concern, how that was reported? Have you ever followed such a -- that processing of the raw material and what it looked like if it was at the higher levels?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The way this is being done is identical in each and every service. So the SDB is no different from any other service. So the same things are done in the FBI and in any other service. Information is received and if it is of interest, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that. But have you ever seen at the FBI what remains in the reporting higher up and what, perhaps, is left out and is dealt with on a more abstract level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. No, of course I've never seen any such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you say to me --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that that's the way it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would not be surprised if it was. But what we therefore, if you say it's the same as with the FBI but you have never seen the FBI practice in this respect, so I return to my question: Did you ever follow on certain incidents the -- the processing of the raw material? Are you describing it in the abstract or do you say, Well, I remember this and this incident, how that was processed, and what remained in the reports when it reached the higher levels? Do you have any practical examples or is it just an abstract description of how you think it was done and how it should have been done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I hope that I'm not supposed to testify here as a fact witness. I cannot really say anything about that. I cannot say that I personally participated in ... if that is what is needed. I mean, I can talk on the basis of the procedure that existed in the service. So, in abstract terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you say, I'm not supposed to testify here as a fact witness. Indeed, you are called primary as an expert. But if would you have any knowledge and you're asked about it, then you're supposed to answer that question on the basis of your personal knowledge. But do I well understand that the process you described from raw material, starting with an incident or a crime but not irrelevant for broader security interests, that you have never personally observed how this material, once verified, once categorised, once processed, what it looked like at the end of the hierarchical journey, that information would make?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, I was not in higher echelons, so I cannot ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, dealing with the 5th Administration very briefly -- no, before we move onto that. Are you able to indicate or cast any light on whether a particular issue -- no. Let me put it differently. It's possible, isn't it, that with this system, as -- a particular security issue or an issue which was considered might impact on security, could circulate within the system for months, if not years, before reaching the upper part of the system, according to the rules?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Theoretically, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The 5th Administration, was this the administration that was responsible for external reporting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: According to the rules, the 5th Administration made the decision after analysis concerning who - for example, the minister of interior, the president of the government or the president of the assembly, and so on - would receive that information; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was sent from the 5th Administration. There was this constant practice of having this sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And so it would -- there was an external reporting team within the 5th Administration who would make that decision; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And it was presumed within the rules that the written reporting externally would be done by the 5th Administration; whereas, the chief of the service would be expected to report orally to the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in principle. As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Would the chief, according to the rules, even know who the relevant or important sources were within the work of the DB?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't have to know. He could have, but he didn't have to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: He could have inquired, but it wasn't presumed that he would be told, according to the rules.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If I could just have a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, apart from giving you that moment, if we go into very details of the rules, I'd very much appreciate to know exactly where it is in the rules that you can ask for information but not automatically receive that, because that's -- because I then would like to know whether it is a specific rule or not. If there's no specific rule, it might well be that the witness is interpreting rather wide rules in his own way without -- without relying on -- on practical information that this is what the rule came down to in reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me move onto paragraph 214 of your report, Mr. Milosevic. And I want to understand a little more about the role of the deputy chief of the service.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I missed something, but I was hoping for the answer to His Honour Judge Orie's question as to which rule the witness was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if that rule is not given then ... it was more guidance for the future than that I asked for that specific rule to be identified. But, of course, it could -- it could assist, Mr. Jordash, if already that specific last matter, if there's a specific rule on it, it would certainly strengthen the answer of the witness. It was about that he could have inquired but that under the rules it was not presumed that he would be told.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you able to -- I know it's a task. Are you able to say which rule that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which specific rule that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- which specific rule you were referring to when you said in principle, "The written reporting would be done by the 5th Administration; whereas, the chief would be expected to report orally..."?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rule on work. The work rule as far as the 5th Administration is concerned. If you allow me, I can explain a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I'm not that much -- I wasn't seeking lengthy explanations but, rather, whether, if it said this was in accordance with the rules, to see how specific the rules. Because if the rules are very specific, then it's self-explanatory. We don't need further explanations. If the rule, however, is not very specific then, of course, it might need further explanation. But first I would like to know what rule. Where do I find that rule so that can I read that rule and see to what extent that rule gives the information I need in order to assess to what extent it was really a matter of following the rules or whether it was that the rules gave more discretion or more liberty to act in the spirit of the rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly. May we return to this to save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please. I leave it in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's deal with another subject and we'll come back to that. I don't want you have to be sitting there panicking looking for rules, but we'll see if we can expedite this in due course. Unless, of course, you have an answer at your fingertips, then feel free.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this pertains to the part of my report that has to do with the work of the 5th Administration. That is where there is a reference to the rules on its work and that is where I talk about that. I don't know if it's necessary for me to go into any more detail than that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No. We'll leave it there for the movement and we shall check that out and I'll come back to you on that. Let's deal now with the chief -- sorry, the deputy chief. I want to try to understand what you were trying to say in paragraphs 214 and 218. You appear to describe a change in 1992 where, in 1991, the deputy chief had a particular position, the office of assistant secretary, and therefore were appointed to the Executive Council of Serbia at the proposal of the republican secretariat minister of the interior, compared with 218 where you describe the deputy and a number of other -- well, and the assistant chiefs as being in the competence of the minister, i.e., an official authorised by him. What does all that mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I think that the interpreter did not interpret this properly. What I heard in the interpretation does not fully correspondence to the facts. It's not that he was elected into the federal Executive Council. It is the federal Executive Council of the government that chose him. I will be very specific on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it is a good custom in this courtroom that if we have problems with translation by our interpreters that we express our concerns and that we repeat what we said so that it in the back of the mind of our interpreters that were the concerns, that it can be -- the same words can be spoken again and then we'll see whether this is any translation problem or not. We are not used to tell that the interpreters did their job wrongly. We are seeking verification. It's raw material, you see, so it needs to be verified, and so, therefore, if you have any concerns, please say exactly or repeat the words you spoke and say that you have concerns, possible concerns about the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. I certainly had no intention of offending anyone or disturbing the work process in general or interfering with the good customs prevailing here. It just seemed to me, as I was listening to the interpretation, that the Defence attorney put a question that was a bit illogical or perhaps the interpretation of his question was a bit illogical, so I kindly ask for the question to be interpreted to me again or to be repeated to me once again, and then I will try to answer. I don't know what the exact custom is here, but I will do my best to comply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash will repeat the question, and listen carefully so that you can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Perhaps I can just simplify it, and you can explain what you meant. What was the change you describe in paragraph 214 and 218 concerning the deputy chief of the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the rules from 1990, the deputy chief of the service was an official who was the assistant to the secretary, that is to say, the minister. He would be appointed by the government, called the Executive Council at the time, and this was at the proposal of the republican secretary, the minister of the interior. In fact, in 1992, at a later date, he was no longer the assistant to the minister. The government did not appoint him. The minister or someone that he authorised, an official that he authorised, would appoint him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So, in 1991, the practical effect of that was that the deputy would report directly to the minister or could report directly to the minister?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All officials, all staff members in the service, whether they had been appointed by the government or the minister, all reported to the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry. When you said "all staff members in the service reported to the minister of the interior," you mean literally or figuratively, or indirectly, through their hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was done within the hierarchy. But they had to carry out any task that they were ordered to carry out.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So the only distinction that you're seeking to make in 214 and 218 is the appointment, the way of appointing the deputy chief; is that right? And the assistant chiefs.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In principle, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to paragraph 225 of your report. I want to try to understand what these sub-laws that you refer to in this paragraph and above meant for the role of the deputy chief? First of all, "preparing and proposing the operative programme of work to -- of the service department and seeing to the realisation of the same from which stems his co-ordinating function vis-a-vis the heads of the organisational units of the SDB/RDB." So that the deputy chief -- the deputy chief played a hands-on role, and the heads of the administration were supposed to report to him and he was supposed to organise and co-ordinate them; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So he was engaged on a day-to-day with the direct co-ordination of the administrations. That was the core of his work, according to the rules?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If, according to the rules, the head of the 8th Administration had a problem with supply of logistics or a manpower problem, his port of call, his first port of call, was the deputy chief; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, yes. Although, the deputy chief was primarily involved in operative affairs, not logistics. But my answer to your question is: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And when you say "operative affairs," you mean what?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
