utterances.text: Well, I mean the duties you mentioned a minute ago. He proposed an operative programme for the service and concerned himself with its implementation and that is the essence of the service's work.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, moving down the paragraph: "Organising the conduct of special actions in conditions of a state of emergency, a threat of war, or war." Special actions include what kind of activities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, by definitions these were actions carried out in extraordinary circumstances or when the security of the country was under threat. And he would then be directly in charge of such actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What does "directly in charge" mean? Does it mean that he would be responsible for ensuring the correct planning of a special action?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The planning and action and for carrying it out. He was directly in charge of officers in the field, and he concerned himself with the implementation of the plan itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: "Concerned himself with the implementation ..." So the special action, let's say, unit, or special action group, would be expected to report to him during -- before, during, and after the special action?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Especially after the action.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Why especially after?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be able to see what the results were. If he was involved in the plan, one would expect there to be feedback, information. That's quite logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And if -- presumably, then, he would be responsible that the special action was properly financed and supplied.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was concerned with such matters, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now we'll come back to that shortly. I wanted just to ask you about one exhibit, a document that's exhibited in this trial, and you may or may not have any information on it because it does deal with some facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: P2990, please, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now it's a report -- Official Note, I should say, concerning supply of weapons and ammunitions which appears to, according to this note, are assigned -- I think it's agreed by Bogdanovic and Tepavcevic. And I was wondering if you're able to cast any light in terms of the rules how the assistant chief, in 1991, was able to, or did, arrange with the minister of the interior to supply weapons and ammunitions to Knin? Do you know anything in the rules that would suppose that the minister would go to the assistant chief for such a thing?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you know Tepavcevic in 1991? Had you heard of him? Or did you know him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd heard of him, and I knew him by sight. But we weren't close.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: He was a -- an older man at that time and a man of long-standing within the DB; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you able to confirm that he was also hugely respected within the service by other members of the DB?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can we have --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm about to ask him how he knows that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How do you know that, Professor?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what was said. He was a person who had authority. I didn't investigate the matter with members of the service in order to see to what extent they respected him, but that is the impression I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you have any information on whether he effectively bypassed the chain of command and went straight to the minister, as this Official Note might suggest?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you able to confirm that he became the deputy of the DB in February of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He became the deputy chief of the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Am I correct that, in terms of facts, you are not able to confirm or otherwise whether Tepavcevic reported faithfully his activities to the chief, Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me move to a slightly different subject, and I'll come back to this in due course. The 8th Administration. The 8th Administration came into existence sometime in 1992. Is that in accordance with your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And it created effectively another layer of administration, in that the joint services, which had existed prior to that, continued to exist, but the DB would obtain its logistics by going through the 8th Administration, which would then go to the joint services. Is that a fair summary?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes. The 8th Administration was involved in logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, what I'm asking is how was it involved in logistics. How did the -- what role did it play? And please indicate whether you're answering from the rules or whether you're answering from your personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of my personal experience, since I was involved in administrative matters in the 8th Administration, so I can just speak about the things that I did, so everything else is on the basis of the rules. The 8th Administration was involved in providing security for buildings, providing protection at gates so to speak, at entrances. Perhaps that's not a nice way of putting. Then it was also involved in solving housing issues for staff members and repairing or obtaining motor vehicles. It was also involved in financial issues, salaries, and so on and so forth. It was also involved in education, and I also dealt with such matters so I know about that. It would organise professional examinations for trainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But each member only knew about his own duties. So I don't know what the finance section or the -- or the transport section did, so I can't testify about that. But can I testify on the basis of the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can you testify to this: That if, for example, the head of an administration, say, Administration 1, wanted resources, wanted vehicles, wanted side-arms, wanted whatever, they would approach the 8th Administration directly and make a request. Is that how it worked?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is so typically an example. I'd like to see the rule, because the witness said that because of his work in the 8th Administration, the only thing he knew what he was doing himself, but he could answer all the other questions on the basis of the rules. So, therefore, I'd like to see the rule which supports the answer. Because the witness's answer was not, that is how it worked. But he said, As a rule, that's how it worked. So I'd like to see that rule, then, to find out, to be able to verify.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But personally I'm not aware of one, but I'll try and find out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. That's my concern. If there is a rule, I'm easily satisfied that the answer is adequately given on the base of that rule; however, if that rule doesn't exist, then there may be a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I was trying to focus the witness on his factual knowledge given that he worked in the 8th Administration because I wasn't aware of a rule and that's why I moved to that, but maybe the witness does know about a rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the last half line before you put this question to the witness, he said: "But I can testify on the basis of the rules." And he explained quite clearly that he could tell us about his personal experience, as far as in the 8th Administration. Now, unless - and that's, of course, important - that you focus him on whether he has any personal experience with this. That's apparently -- because then the answer: "As a rule, yes," is that he experienced that this usually happened, or is it on the basis of the rules that is how it should happen? That's the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Professor, are we talking about a specific rule, about the heads of administration reporting to the -- sorry, making a direct request to the 8th Administration? Are you unable to point to a rule but point to practice?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the rules on work are the only rules I can refer you to. But I personally can't testify about that since I wasn't in the leadership of the 8th Administration. I wasn't part of the management team, so I didn't receive or authorise any of the requests. The entire service functioned on the basis of the rules of work. The rules on organisation and job specifications. But I don't know whether there is a particular rule. I haven't heard about it, and I didn't find any such rule in the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So do you have any personal knowledge, then, of the way in which the heads of administration or any other relevant personnel would obtain supplies from the 8th Administration or via the 8th Administration?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't testify about that. I don't know. Requests would, in general, be submitted in writing, but, no, I really can't make any claims. To the extent that I can testify about this, requests were made in written form. But I really cannot testify about something that I did not participate in.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, what -- what would you do if you wanted or needed supplies, personally?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would contact the 8th Administration, make a request, and explain why I needed certain items. It wouldn't be the matter of my whim. It would be something that was necessary in operative terms. So I would submit a request and explain why I was making the request. That is how I would have acted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Who would you make the request to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, now the witness has testified that he has no experience with it, he has no personal knowledge. He doesn't know about specific rules. We are now, more or less, inviting him to invent a situation. Why is what this witness would do be any more relevant than what Ms. Marcus would do under the circumstances or what you would do yourself under the circumstances? He is called as an expert witness. Apparently his expertise doesn't help him out. Then he might have knowledge because he worked in the system. He says, I don't have one. I don't have that knowledge. And then we start, What would do you if. Is that -- is that a proper question to put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, it's not the -- I wasn't intend -- if I conveyed that I was asking a hypothetical, then that's my sloppy language. I was exactly asking him what he actually did. Presumably, he required supplies at some point during his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- occupation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know. Ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you require supplies during your time at the 8th Administration or your time before the 8th Administration?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't necessary for me to have supplies of any kind in order to perform the duties that I had to perform. Therefore, I did not contact the 8th Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you ever receive per diems?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Let's leave the subject there then. If you can't assist, you can't. Let's go into paragraph 200, please. Now, we -- I want to discuss with you special purpose resources. Let's go straight to the instruction for the use and control of distribution of funds for special expenses.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have on the screen, please -- or perhaps we can deal with the report itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In paragraph 201: "The special expenditure resources ... were determined by the annual estimate of special purposes [sic] resources of the republican secretariat/Ministry of Interior." Were these decided at a meeting of the government or where would they be determined?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would be determined at the collegium of the republican secretariat. The ministry -- it was at the top level of the ministry that these decisions were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have on the screen, please, 2D937. These are the instructions themselves. Let's go straight to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now in paragraph 1 on page 2 of the B/C/S and page 2 of the English, paragraph 1 states: "These instructions regulate the use and control of distribution of funds for special expenses ..." And then further: "With the exception of use and distribution which is in compliance with the law, carried out in a manner determined by the Executive Council of the Assembly of the SR of Serbia?" Can you cast light on what was the anticipated role described here of the Executive Council?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Paragraph -- sorry, item 6: "The funds in dinars --"

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May we have a break, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break and will resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked to start without the witness. The Chamber is very worried about the present situation where it takes an enormous amount of time to find out what the witness doesn't know. That's -- and that's not only in your examination, Mr. Jordash, but I think whenever you would want to elicit any evidence of fact, the witness says I do not appear as a witness of fact. I think I explained to him clearly that if he knows anything, if asked about it, then he should come. At the same time, we could not have after the experience we have over the last few days a high expectations as far as the factual knowledge of the witness, and the Chamber is unanimous in that we should, whenever we want to elicit anything else than a reproduction of rules and the context of rules and when they were adopted, that we should first establish whether the witness is able to tell us anything. Mr. Jordash, if you would conclude your cross-examination in the next session, which I hope you would do, would you net -- not have your three-hour, but, nevertheless, the Chamber would like to limit you to the next session. Some of my questions have assisted in being able to move on a bit. So the other parties keep this in mind for the continuation of the evidence of this witness. Of course, I can't tell exactly what you should and what you shouldn't ask, but I think -- do we call this learning on the job? That's what I would like you to do, is to learn very much on this job. Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. If I look at the list of the source material, I see that, at the very end of the list, not only a 65 ter number appears but also an exhibit number, D228. I'd like to draw the attention of the parties to the fact that D228 was marked, not admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And therefore, it cannot be just relied upon by referring to this exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm going to try to shortcut things so that we can move a bit more swiftly, Professor. Let's go to paragraph 203 of your report, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have it on the screen, please. Just find the ... 2D00 -- it's there, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: 203. As I read this, I see you, on the basis of the rules, make a distinction between the way in which special expenditure resources was dealt with and the way in which foreign means of payment was dealt with; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the way it is in the regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you define "special resources" elsewhere in the report, but it includes, does it not, the issuance of resources for the engagement of associates?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So the distinction you draw from the rules in relation to, inter alia, the issuance of resources for associates as compared to foreign means of payment is that the first can be dealt with by personnel authorised by the chief, whereas the foreign means of payment remain tightly within the authority of the chief as an individual?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can put it that way too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, how would you put it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As is written here. That is to say, special expenditure resources in dinars, that is to say the domestic currency, were handled by an employee so authorised by the chief; that is to say, at headquarters. Whereas, in other administrative units, it was employees who were authorised to do that by their supervisors because it is only natural to do this at the level of all organisational units, because the chief of the service itself would be way too busy if he were to authorise all of that. This is simply inherited from the days when everything went through the SDB of the SSUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You told us before the break that the chief did not have to know who the associates were; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Every associate was kept under a certain code. This was done for the following reasons --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- so that no one would know who this individual actually was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Actually, yes. Sorry, I sorry to interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm interested in this. Please continue that description.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That means that he received reports and he could receive some information that had been provided by that associate under his pseudonym. So if he really wanted to, he could have insisted, but it simply wasn't customary to ask for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And from what you've just said, also, it certainly wasn't practical because we are talking about a service with hundreds of -- if not thousands of associates. So to expect under the rules the chief to know who each and every associate was, would not be practical; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wouldn't be possible. There's too much of all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Why -- why was there a distinction with the foreign means of payment, according to the rules? What did the -- was -- was there a rule which dealt with foreign means of payment? Because paragraph 203 isn't footnoted at this point, when you deal with foreign means of payment.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. There is no reference to the footnote. This goes back to the times when foreign exchange transactions went only through the federal organs, the federal Ministry of Interior, that was quite simply in charge of everything that had to do with foreign countries. So, from that point of view, you see for yourself that it says the SDB of the SSUP. So this is a regulation that was taken over, inherited, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you have any information concerning whether the deputy chief whose job was to implement the special-purposes actions was authorised to deal with the special-purposes resources during 1991 to 1995? And I'm asking you a factual question.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that that's the way it was, but I don't have any proof. I don't know. I cannot confirm that as a witness. It would be logical for it to be that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, why it would be logical?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he was in charge of these operative actions, if we can put it that way, and it would be logical for him to take care of that. But this is my opinion. I cannot actually invoke any kind of experience here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm not going to push you on it. Now, looking at the instruction for the use and control of distribution of funds, I want to try to summarise - and please correct me if I'm wrong in my summary - the role of the chief. The role of the chief was to help to decide on the overall annual budget - correct? - for the special purposes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: To authorise for special purposes funds, subordinates to deal directly with them; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And, according to item 17, which we can turn to, if you want, of these rules, "to form a committee appointed by the chief of security, to control the use of the resources for special expenses in the basic organisational units of the State Security Services once a year." Let's turn to that so we have it in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: 2D00937, please. Let's go to paragraph 7 -- or item 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: There, you have it in front of you. And the committee's role, according to this rule, was to make inspections and submit a report on the proposal of the chief of the service. So according to the rule, am I correct the chief was not presumed to be accessing the actual documentation detailing the allocation of resources but was supposed to be receiving a report from a committee who oversaw the issuance of the resources; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's this internal commission that had that task. They did not deal with all the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, let's have a look at -- we -- we haven't had translated until now when we've translated it -- item 14. "Chief of the State Security Service may authorise chiefs of primary organisational units to approve payments of means for special expenditures; namely: ..." And I won't read out. But, effectively, this is the allocation of authority by the rules to subordinate members of the state security to deal with these special-purpose funds - is that right? - up to certain amounts?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right. And that is strictly in accordance with the rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, may I seek clarification of one of the previous answers, which I did not fully understand. Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Jordash asked you, and I read again the question. Mr. Jordash asked whether he was correct when he said that the chief was not presumed to be accessing the actual documentation, detailing the allocation of resources but was supposed to be receiving a report from a committee who oversaw the issuance of the resources, and asked whether that was a correct understanding. Your answer was: "That's correct. That is this internal commission that had this task. They did not deal with all the details." Now the question by Mr. Jordash was more or less suggesting that the chief would not deal with the details but read the report. Now you say that's correct. That was the task of that commission, and they did not deal with the details. So I've now -- apparently the commission is not dealing with the details, and, at the same time, the chief is not dealing with the details; but, nevertheless, relies on a report, which is supposed to be based on -- on a detailed review. Yeah, I was a bit confused about the "they," they are supposed not to deal with the details.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is what this is about. Actually, I don't dare say this, obviously. I mean, I'll explain this answer. All right. I'm not going to criticise the interpreters that they misinterpret. So the chief of service did not deal with all the details. He just dealt with the report, whereas the commission dealt with all the details. It is my mistake if I did not state this clearly enough, but I think that I've clarified it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say the commission did deal with the details but the chief did not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me just ask you very briefly about the JATD in the context that we're discussing. A witness here, I think, was public. No, he wasn't public, so I'll keep ... D409, a witness here said the following at paragraph 49. This is a witness who was involved in the JATD, and he said: "Requests for per diems were signed by the deputy commander of the JATD. The administration of the unit would process such requests and send them to the 8th Administration." Then: "Based on the approval of Deputy Chief Tepavcevic, one would procure the money from the administration for the joint matters of the MUP." Did you follow that? I can repeat that, if you want.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I fully understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: From your knowledge of the rules, would that testimony be entirely consistent with the presumptions laid out in the rules for the expense -- or allocation of resources for special purposes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Reserve forces, I want to just ask you briefly about them. You --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are we leaving the area of the expenditures or --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I ask, then, one question, so as to better understand. Mr. Milosevic, I looked at this document about the instructions for the use and the control of funds for special expenditures or expenses. And if I read number 1 -- could we have that on our screen? We're still with the same document we used before. Could we go to the first page, also in English, yes, the first paragraph. The instructions start by saying that they regulate the use and the control of distribution, et cetera, so it explains what it does. And then the second part of the first sentence reads as follows: "... with the exception of use and distribution which is, in compliance with the law, carried out in a manner determined by the Executive Council of the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Serbia." If I read this, it sounds as these are the instructions, how to do it, with the exception of a situation where it was determined that it would be done otherwise. That's what, at first glance, seems to be -- so we do it in accordance with this rule, or if it's determined otherwise, we'll do it otherwise. Could you shed some light on this exception and whether you have -- know of any examples of this exception being applied or any documentary evidence on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I've already answered that I don't know. I can assume a certain situation, if that would be relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Unless you have specific basis for making such an assumption, then I would -- it might come down to speculation, which I would like to avoid. Which means that paying a lot of attention to this document, which starts by saying, This is how we'll do it unless we do it otherwise. Have you any comment on my interpretation of this first sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, for example, if there were some major expenditures involved like renovating a building or something, then the Minister of the Interior had to give his consent. Perhaps that is what is meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't it true that the document specifically deals with the immovable property so that that is included in those rules?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I would be speculating. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't invite you to do it, but since you did it, I respond to that. If have you no further comments, I'll invite Mr. Jordash to proceed. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We have just been discussing the allocation of special-purposes funds, and the example I offered was the allocation of funds in the circumstances where associates were being engaged. If reserve forces were being engaged for special purposes, would you expect -- would you anticipate that they would fall within the instruction for the use and control of distribution of funds that we've been looking at? That's a long way of saying: Are reserve forces included and governed by this instruction, if they're employed for special purposes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These resources concerned, above all, certain rewards given to associates. It was less frequent or almost never done for associates, but sometimes associates were rewarded from those resources [as interpreted]. These resources were also used for certain expenses incurred by operative officers when they had contact with associates and other sources; for example, citizens, operative connections. So that was the basis upon which these resources were allocated, these special resources were allocated. But I really can't answer your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the second sentence in the answer in the last answer given by the witness doesn't make much sense, I think. Perhaps it wasn't correctly recorded, what the witness said wasn't correctly recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to verify. You referred to certain rewards given to associates. And then - and I read now our transcript, and please correct when you think that you said something else: "It was less frequent or almost never done for associates, but sometimes associates were rewarded from those resources." Is that what you said or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you then please repeat that last -- that line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was very seldom or almost -- associates were almost never paid when they were engaged. It was quite infrequent. But regardless to how they were engaged, they were occasionally rewarded. So I don't know how to put it more precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say associates were now and then rewarded from those resources but they didn't get a regular payment. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I'll try and explain this to make it clearer. May I? So earlier on, when testifying, I said that associates could be engaged on various bases. The material motive was only one such basis. Such an associate was naturally remunerated immediately after having been engaged, but occasionally other associates could be remunerated, other associates who had been engaged on some other basis, on any other basis. The other purpose of these resources was to reimburse certain expenses incurred by an operative officer in the course of establishing contact with an associate, or an agent, or some other source in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. May we turn to item 7 in these instructions so I can try to repeat my question about reserve forces. 7(1) states that the special use of funds, includes: "... work with operative positions of the service, allowances and awards for associates and other persons who provide information and intelligence of interest to the service, operative actions, and other activities of the State Security Service." My question is: Is your understanding of that rule, that special-purpose expenses could be allocated pursuant to this rule to reserve forces engaged in operative actions, on behalf of the state security.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't answer that question in concrete terms. Under (5) [as interpreted] you have a very general phrase. It says there the other operatives and operative and analytic work. So this is a very general way of putting things. It doesn't allow one to make an exhaustive list, so I can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, the reference to paragraph (5) came as a bit of a surprise to me, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I think we have a problem with the interpretation. Item (5) was not adequately interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you referred to the very general phrase, you referred to what paragraph of these instructions Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, under item (7), we have a list of everything that is included and then it mentions another list.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Mr. Petrovic's comment perhaps concerned the written translation itself and the adequacy of the written translation in item 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it may be, and that's exactly the reason why -- interpretation and transcription, of course, they work closely together, and sometimes if there is any question, we might not always be able to know exactly where the problem lies, and therefore, rather focus on resolving the problem than to find out what -- who may have done something wrong by not pronouncing the words well, by a slip of the tongue in translation, or a slip of the fingers in transcribing. That's, again, I'm, as always, expressing my surprise that it happens only so little. When I asked you to which paragraph you referred, the simple answer would therefore be paragraph (7). And that's understood. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me ask you this then: Apart from this instruction, for the use and control of special-purpose funds, were you aware of any other instruction, regulation, or law, which allowed the allocation of special-purpose funds existing between 1991 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's have on the screen, please, P2401. I'm moving to another subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your last question --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In view of the earlier matter which I raised with the witness, your last question is a bit ambiguous and I'd like to know exactly what the witness tells us. Mr. Jordash asked were you aware of any other instruction, regulation, or law. Now, we earlier discussed the beginning of this instruction, which says, This is how we do it, or unless we decide to do it otherwise. When you said you were not aware of anything, were you focussing on any -- any document you have found? And can you tell us that there are no laws with different instructions? Or do you say, I'm not aware of it but I might not have a complete image of what may be there in terms of legislation? And the second issue I would like to raise with you, whether the exception provided for clearly in the first sentence of this instruction, whether you can positively affirm that it was never done in the other way described there, or that you say, Well, may have happened, but I'm not aware of it. So, first: Rule, laws, regulations, well, let's say published. Can you positively affirm that they do not exist? Or do you say, I did not come across any of -- any law, any regulation which would deal with the same matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not familiar with any such documents. I never came across such documents. As for the second part of your question, I haven't fully understood it, so could you please clarify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, here we have an instruction; that's a written instruction. Mr. Jordash was, first of all, asking about other laws. I do understand laws to be written documents, published, regulations which might not have to be public. But regulations of a general validity. Whereas, in paragraph 1, reference is made to an exception, although in compliance with the law, but use and distribution carried out in a manner determined by the Executive Council of the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Serbia. Which I understand could also be an incidental determination of doing it differently so not in the kind of a rule with general validity but, rather, on a very specific occasion. Because that's, for me, the difference between laws and regulations. They have a kind of a general validity, whereas to determine that you do it otherwise does not need to have a general character -- do not need to have the character of general validity. If you say, Neither rules nor laws nor such a determination I am aware of, then that would answer my question. If, however, you would be aware of anything, either in the field of legislation, regulations, or in the field of the exceptions, as referred to in the first sentence of paragraph 1, please let me know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not familiar with any such cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I want to deal very swiftly with this issue of Stanisic and him being appointed to the position of chief. Because you gave an answer on the 3rd of May --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honours, page 18972.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- which might be considered to be ambiguous. What was your understanding of when Stanisic became the chief of the DB? Was it consistent with this appointment we see in front of us?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a fact that he was first appointed -- I apologise. I can't see this very clearly. I'll have to have another look at it. Yes, that's the decision in which he was appointed as the chief of the SDB of the RSUP, and he was appointed to the position of an advisor. The date of this decision is the 31st of December, 1991. So from the date that this decision entered into force, he was in that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know what his position was before that? I'm asking you a factual question, if you know.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on then. Let's have a look, if we can, at page 2 of the English. And if we can go up to the bottom of the page in the B/C/S. This is a decision, as we can see, indicating Stanisic became chief on this date. And at the end it says: "This decision is to be sent: To the employee, the administration for material and financial affairs, and the administration for personnel and work relations of this ministry." Now, I looked at the rules on staff planning -- let me -- let me shortcut this. The -- are you able to assist -- in relation to the administration for material and financial affairs at the time of this decision and the administration for personnel and work relations of this ministry at the time of this decision, do you know whether they were situated within the DB or were these more broad Ministry of Interior departments or sections or however they were termed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they weren't integral parts of the SDB. They were part of the joint services. They were, in fact, within the MUP, the Ministry of Interior. So these were organisational units of the Ministry of Interior, not of the SDB.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And do you -- do you -- do you know why such a decision would be sent to the administration for material and financial affairs and the personnel and work relations?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's quite logical. In order to work out the salaries and pay the salaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: To -- so the -- such a decision -- let me start that again. These administrations were principally concerned with the issuance of salaries; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Amongst other things concerned with paying salaries. The administration for these financial matters dealt with all such matters; buying cars, other equipment, and so on and so forth. It wasn't only involved in paying salaries, but in this particular case salaries are referred to. But the administration for personnel and work relations was concerned with personnel files and it was responsible for appointments within the ministry and for termination of employment within the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. And you would expect - is this right? - such a decision would only be sent to, as it states, the employee it concerns and these administrations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says quite explicitly in the decision. Have a look at the last paragraph: "This decision is to be sent to ..." And then it says to whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have on the screen, please, P2403.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is under seal as the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You were shown this -- I think you were shown this document by my learned friend for the Prosecution, and it's the retroactive decision suggesting that Simatovic had been sent to Kosovo during certain dates. Now, if we turn to page 2, please, of the English, would it be logical to you that this decision, likewise being sent to the material and financial affairs administration, would have something to do with salaries?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you wouldn't expect if this document was, as you've just said, was placed within a file with a clear decision that it go only to these internal administrations and to the employee that anyone else would see it; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So the -- the -- the fraud suggested by the Prosecution would logically be a fraud on the internal administrations we see mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Yes. If it's a fraud, because I don't know the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you able to confirm that at the time of this decision, if one was sent to Kosovo, one would be able to apply to the material and financial affairs administration for an uplift in salary and an increase in expenses?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whoever was sent to assist in Kosovo would receive a high salary because there would be other expenses incurred by living there. So anyone who was sent to work in Kosovo requested that such expenses be covered.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know if that was covered by -- let's go back to the first page, please, of this document in English and the top of the page in the B/C/S. Are you able to confirm that these salary issues and expenses issues were dealt with by the Law on Internal Affairs, Article 72, and the special edition number 4/90 and authorisation 01 number 1130/91-2, these regulations and laws dealt with this issue of an uplift in salary and expenses? Are you able to confirm that or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. If you refer to all these articles in the introduction, one could say that that is the basis for increasing the salaries. The employee didn't make such a request. The administration would provide that increase. It wasn't necessary for the employee to constantly make requests. If there was a legal basis for this to be done, then the employee would receive his, or her, salary on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you aware of any law or order or such that would have mandated the paying of a higher salary or expenses if personnel, such as Simatovic, was working in Croatia or Bosnia at the time of this decision? Was there anything governing the paying of expenses in those locations? Or the paying of salaries.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, finally, I want to ask you about a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Please, could we have on the screen 1D01231.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is a related but it is a different subject. If you take some time just to read the decision, dated 2nd of July, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think we need to go over the page as well, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm just wondering ... okay. I'm sorry, I was looking at a different document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We were -- I'll -- you were discussing with my learned friend from the Prosecution previously what the Serbian DB was or was not authorised to do outside of Serbia. Were you aware of this decision by the minister of the interior at the behest of the government or to -- to allow the DB to operate in the way suggested outside of Serbia? Operation Pauk but a different Pauk to what we're used to.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of this decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I -- we don't know what the provenance is of this document, but if it came from the Serbian authorities, then perhaps in an abundance of caution it shouldn't be broadcast. It looks like an official DB document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, it's your document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm content with it being public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You were not aware of this decision anyway. Is that what you said, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I apply to bar table this decision, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'd like to have information, please, about the provenance of the document. We don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It was a document which the accused, Mr. Stanisic, had, and he gave it to the Office of the Prosecutor in 2003 during his interviews.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In that case, I am afraid it suffers from that problem of coming from the accused's personal collection and we object. If the Defence wants to try to obtain the original, it can be MFI'd, perhaps, until they can obtain it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm not going to get into the previous discussions, but I'm happy for it to be MFI'd and we'll do what we can to provide further information, but our position is that it's sufficiently -- it crosses the threshold but we're content with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I know that there is a debate, a dispute about the documents which were provided by Mr. Stanisic. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1231 will receive number D796, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. When we were talking about documents, we had a look P2401 recently, Ms. Marcus, I noticed that most likely there are parts missing in the translation. I, for example, see a clear reference to the date the 1st of January, 1992, in the original, whereas at the same place I do not find anything in the English translation. Further, there's handwriting at the bottom of that document which is also not reflected in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'll check that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it's not that it may change things that dramatically, but there's always a risk that if the translation is not accurate that it affects in one way or another the document. Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have on the screen, D113.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And this, Professor, is the final very brief subject I want to ask you about. It's related to the last subject --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry, again.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Whilst that's coming up, it was suggested to you by the Prosecution that if the DB were deploying individuals to Croatia and Bosnia in 1991 and 1995, to participate in joint combat operations, they would have to create documents to conceal this deployment in order to fit into the rules and regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, page 19010.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about D113, and in particular Article -- or item, I think it's item 3. Yes, Article 3. Page 3 of the English and page 4 of the B/C/S. And if you would just read Article 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And just for context to assist Your Honours, this is a set of rules which are dated January 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And if you just read -- you've already read that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If we go over the page in the English and we should stay on page 4 of the B/C/S. In fact, no, let's go to page 5 of the B/C/S. And it states there - and this is the particular bit I want to direct your attention to: "Other republic security duties are in particular the duties of providing counter-intelligence protection to republican organs, organising and carrying out preparations for defence and work in case of an imminent threat of war and in war, preparing appropriate contributions to the plan for the defence of the republic, planning and co-ordinating the duties of protecting facilities, areas, and workplaces important for the defence of the republic, and organising and providing cryptographic data protection and special-purpose communication [sic]." Now, keeping that in mind, Professor, a Prosecution witness, JF-095, from the state security, agreed that that provision would have permitted the state security of Serbia to form such military units as the JATD.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Page 7096.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you agree with that interpretation, that this would have enabled, by law, the DB to create the JATD?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in view of the wording here, it could be put that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the JATD, from the wording, would then -- or could have been used to organise and carry out preparations for defence? I'll leave it at that. No more questions. Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash. I'm looking at the clock. I don't think it makes much sense to continue your cross-examination. Unless you have a limited series of questions, Ms. Marcus, which you could easily put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'm in the Chamber's hands, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you could feel five minutes in a meaningful way and not being stopped halfway in the middle of a subject, then you are invited to do so, and if you say no, I can't, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I think I can do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please proceed. Ms. Marcus will now continue her cross-examination for a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a few questions about the section of Franko Simatovic of your report, which is part 8. And in that section, in addition to describing the documents contained in Mr. Simatovic's personnel file, you make several factual assertions as well. In paragraph 338, for example, you state in relation to Mr. Simatovic that he: "Discharged the duties and tasks of deputy chief of the 2nd RDB Administration." You state in paragraph 356 that: "From the above description of the duties and tasks of special advisor to the chief of the DB, which Franko Simatovic discharged from May 1993 to April 1996," et cetera. Your factual assertions appear not to question that Mr. Simatovic was, in fact, carrying out the duties and responsibilities strictly according to the decisions you analysed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic is on his feet. I do not know whether -- Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have a problem with the very beginning of the question; namely, the assertion that these are facts. Factual allegations. These are actually claims based on the personnel file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's comment on the question. Ms. Marcus, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, your assertions, in addition, appear to presume that the circumscribed duties and responsibilities restricted Mr. Simatovic's ability to do anything else. And that's what I'd like to ask you a little bit about. First, let's take paragraph 369.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- wouldn't it be better to first try to understand what the witness meant in those paragraphs because that might resolve a lot of matters. When you said in these two -- two paragraphs which were read to you by Ms. Marcus that Mr. Simatovic discharged his duties as, did you mean to say that those were the duties he was supposed to -- to perform, to discharge of those duties, or did you want to indicate that he really did that, or was it just, This is what the rule says, and what his duties were, he was in that position so he must have discharged them. Which of the two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, these are the duties that he had to carry out in accordance with the decision on his appointment. He actually had to behave in accordance with that decision. He could not decide whether he wanted to do that or not. He had to do it. Whether he did something else as well, that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or even whether he did what he had to do. You never verified whether he discharged his duties.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, this at least gives, I think, a better understanding of the word "discharge." The witness did not intend to express it -- his opinion in the way you understood it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I agree. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Would Your Honour like to pause at this point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think this is the right moment. We will adjourn for the day. Mr. Milosevic, it may become a bit boring, but I again have to remind you that you should not speak or communicate in any other way with anyone about your testimony, whether given or still to be given. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning. Let me just check that. Yes. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning, the 9th of May, at 9.00 in this same courtroom, II. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
